title: Correction: Neurophysiological signatures of Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy in treatment resistant depression.
Shared cortical morphometry and molecular signatures across depression and physical diseases.
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is highly comorbid with physical diseases, suggesting shared neurobiological mechanisms. However, the common structural and molecular substrates underlying this comorbidity remain poorly understood. We analyzed multimodal MRI data from 577 patients (MDD, asthma, fibromyalgia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, type 2 diabetes) and 275 healthy controls, constructed individual morphometric similarity networks (MSN) to identify shared cortical alterations, and applied principal component analysis with multiscale molecular annotation (transcriptomic, cell-type, neurotransmitter, and cognitive mapping) to characterize underlying mechanisms. All patient groups exhibited regional MSN abnormalities. A shared MSN pattern emerged, featuring increased similarity in visual and somatomotor regions and decreased similarity in ventral attention, limbic, and default mode networks, and was replicated in independent cohorts. This pattern was significantly associated with spatial gene expression enriched for synaptic signaling, membrane potential regulation, and neuronal architecture, with predominant expression in excitatory/inhibitory neurons and astrocytes. It further mapped onto specific neurotransmitter systems, with exploratory cognitive decoding suggesting possible relevance to emotion and social cognition. Related genes overlapped with known risk loci for Alzheimer's disease and bipolar disorder. These findings identify a robust across diseases cortical MSN phenotype linked to convergent molecular and neurochemical correlates, offering a framework for studying shared vulnerability and transdiagnostic mechanisms across depression and physical diseases.

title: Multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM): a reconfigurable platform for high-resolution light-sheet fluorescence microscopy.
abstract: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) enables gentle, rapid and efficient volumetric imaging of biological specimens. Despite its potential, LSFM has fragmented into multiple variants, each narrowly optimized for specific samples or imaging regimes, limiting its broad applicability. Here we introduce the multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM), an adaptable LSFM platform for high-resolution imaging ranging from subcellular dynamics to whole organisms and cleared tissues. miOPM supports seamless interchangeability of oil, water and air objectives and maintains diffraction-limited performance across a refractive index range of 1.33 to 1.51. It is compatible with standard sample mounting, current clearing protocols and high-throughput 3D imaging. We leverage miOPM to image diverse biological specimens at multiple spatial scales. By expanding the adaptability and ease of use of LSFM, miOPM is poised to democratize advanced 3D imaging.

title: Trait judgements of faces using a task without word labels.
abstract: People attribute psychological traits to faces. Previous research has typically elicited these judgements using specific words provided in advance by the experimenter (for example, ratings on competence or trustworthiness), raising questions about completeness (these tasks use a limited set of words) and generalizability (for example, across languages). Here we asked over 3,000 participants to spatially arrange unfamiliar faces based on perceived trait similarity, without providing any word labels. Using predominantly White faces, experiment 1 yielded five dimensions that we interpreted as approachability, gender-specific warmth, competence, morality and youthfulness. Using White, Black and Asian faces, experiment 2 also produced five dimensions, which showed prominent effects of stereotypes associated with race. Comparisons with four other studies that used word labels argue that approachability or warmth emerges as a universal evaluative factor that integrates multiple trait facets (such as trustworthiness, warmth and competence) into a single holistic dimension and that race and gender stereotypes emerge depending on the set of face stimuli used.

title: Machine learning image analysis predicts Parkinson disease genotype and mitochondrial lysosomal abnormalities in iPS neurons.
abstract: Mitochondrial and lysosomal dysfunction are central features of Parkinson's disease (PD) across major genetic forms including PRKN, SNCA, and LRRK2. We applied cell morphomics, a machine-learning-based framework combining high-content imaging with quantitative feature extraction, to analyse mitochondrial and lysosomal morphology at single-cell resolution in iPS cell-derived cortical neurons from PD patients and healthy controls (13 lines total). Supervised machine-learning models distinguished PD neurons from controls with high accuracy (AUC = 0.87) and reliably separated individual genotypes. Feature importance and attribution analysis revealed genotype-specific organelle biases in the relative contribution of mitochondrial and lysosomal features, with mitochondrial features dominating classification in PRKN neurons, balanced mitochondrial and lysosomal contributions in SNCA neurons, and a greater lysosomal contribution in LRRK2 neurons. Multi-class models retained strong performance, and findings were reproduced across two independent laboratories using different dyes and imaging conditions. These results demonstrate that morphomics provides a robust and scalable framework to quantify genotype-specific organelle abnormalities in PD neurons and supports its application for cellular stratification and biomarker discovery.

title: Microglia and border-associated macrophages play opposite roles in cerebrovascular and leukocyte responses under systemic inflammation in male mice.
abstract: Microglia closely associate with the vasculature, but their roles in leukocyte trafficking and cerebral blood flow (CBF) during systemic inflammation are unclear. We show that sustained systemic inflammation leads to altered microglia-vascular interactions, leukocyte recruitment to cerebral blood vessels and reduced hypercapnia-induced vasodilation. We find that microglia and border-associated macrophages (BAMs) play distinct roles in these processes: while BAM depletion with clodronate increases leukocyte recruitment, microglia/BAM depletion with PLX5622 and the absence of microglia, but not BAMs in CSF1RΔFIRE/ΔFIRE mice, result in markedly reduced leukocyte recruitment. Supporting this, conditional microglial IL-1 deletion inhibits leukocyte recruitment. Unlike BAM depletion, the absence of microglia impairs hypercapnia-induced vasodilation, while in vivo two-photon imaging reveals microglial IL-1α-dependent interactions between leukocytes and penetrating arteries. Accordingly, reduced hypercapnia-induced vasodilation involves endothelial IL-1R1 and microglial IL-1α. Thus, distinct brain macrophage populations exert opposite effects on leukocyte recruitment and CBF through IL-1 dependent mechanisms in given vascular beds in male mice.

title: Dynamic gene expression signatures predict psychotherapy response in PTSD.
abstract: Static blood-based biomarkers provide limited insight into psychiatric illness and recovery, largely because they capture only a single, unperturbed snapshot of inherently dynamic biological systems. In this study, we applied a dynamic, longitudinal dual-state approach to characterize peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) transcriptional trajectories associated with psychotherapy outcomes in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). PBMC transcriptional profiles were generated for veterans with PTSD (n = 46, 21, and 17, respectively) and controls (n = 26, 26, and 23) at pre-treatment, post-treatment, and follow-up. The PTSD cohort with profiles across all three timepoints was divided into responders (n = 6) and non-responders (n = 11) based on their Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 (CAPS-5) trajectories. All subjects were profiled in both unstimulated and dexamethasone-stimulated states. At pre-treatment, unstimulated responders and non-responders exhibited pronounced transcriptional differences exceeding those observed between PTSD and controls. Longitudinally, unstimulated responders showed a marked shift toward control-like profiles, whereas non-responders retained persistent divergence. Pathway analyses identified a prominent temporal signal within Class C/3 G-protein-coupled receptor pathways driven largely by bitter taste receptors (TAS2Rs), along with subgroup-specific regulation of GABAB, opioid, and NMDA receptor signaling. Dexamethasone-induced responses further differentiated subgroups and showed opposing associations with recovery trajectories, implicating glucocorticoid sensitivity as a potential predictor of treatment outcomes. These findings indicate that biological responsiveness itself constitutes a measurable phenotype of recovery, and that dynamic functional profiling of living immune cells can reveal clinically relevant trajectories and candidate mechanisms not accessible through static biomarkers.

title: Uncoupling of the allosteric signalling network in the β1-adrenergic receptor by a negative allosteric modulator.
abstract: Allosteric modulation is a fundamental aspect of G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) regulation where molecules that bind to alternative sites outside the orthosteric pocket alter agonist-induced signalling responses. The advantages of allosteric modulators over traditional orthosteric agonists have positioned them as highly promising therapeutic agents. GPCRs exist in tuneable equilibria between multiple functional states, yet the ways in which allosteric modulators reshape these equilibria remain incompletely understood. Here we characterise how changes to the allosteric signalling network influence the conformational dynamics of the β1-adrenergic receptor (β1AR) through mutations at the E1303.41 position or using the negative allosteric modulator, AS408. Both act through a known transmembrane (TM)3-TM4-TM5 site, reducing signalling to similar extents, but through distinct molecular mechanisms as revealed by pharmacological assays, MD simulations, and solution nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. E1303.41 mutations reduce agonist-stimulated signalling as a side chain-dependent rheostat, shifting receptor equilibria to populate states with weaker G protein affinities. In contrast, AS408 uncouples the intracellular region of β1AR from the influence of the orthosteric pocket and reduces G protein coupling by adoption of an alternative signalling-incompetent intracellular surface arrangement. Our investigations emphasise the relevance of mechanistic understanding in drug development and the importance of dynamics in GPCR allostery.

title: Predicting trail-making test performance using 7-Tesla structural cerebral MRI.
abstract: Psychopharmaceutical therapy has seen a lack of improvement in efficacy, highlighting the need for a more individualized treatment approach that optimally leverages pharmaceutical effects. To achieve this, it is necessary to identify factors that can predict psychological attributes and treatment outcomes. We hypothesize that brain morphology may serve as a predictor of performance in psychological tests. A 7-Tesla-MRI system was used to measure 74 transdiagnostic patients and 41 healthy controls. Values for grey matter volume (GMV), cortical thickness and gyrification based on the Schaefer 100 Atlas for parcellation were determined. Using this morphological data, performance in a Trail-Making Test (TMT) - A and B was predicted with the help of a deep learning model. A SHAP analysis was conducted to identify the key variables important for the model. The accuracy in predicting TMT performance was very good at 0.795. The most decisive feature influencing predictions was gyrification. Areas indicating inter-group differences were focused in the frontal cortex, as well as in temporal and parietal regions. Morphological characteristics can predict test performance with high accuracy. These results support the implementation of a transdiagnostic approach in clinical practice to better address the underlying pathophysiology. Symptom prediction based on neuroimaging data appears to be an achievable goal.

title: Imaging nanoscopic co-assemblies of α-synuclein and Tau in human samples.
abstract: α-synuclein (αS), amyloid-β (Aβ), and Tau aggregates are hallmarks of many neurodegenerative diseases, yet the prevalence and nature of their nanoscopic co-assemblies remain poorly understood. Here, we adapt a single-molecule pull-down (SiMPull) assay to profile αS, Aβ, and Tau co-assemblies across post-mortem brain tissue homogenates, soluble brain fractions, human serum, cerebrospinal fluid, and saliva. We show that αS-Tau co-assemblies are abundant across all sample matrices, accounting for ~10-70% of total αS aggregates in both Parkinson's disease (PD) and control samples. Notably, αS-Tau co-assemblies in soluble brain fractions from controls exhibit higher Proteinase K (PK) resistance than those from PD cases. Biophysically, Tau accelerates αS aggregation in simple in vitro systems, but this effect is suppressed in complex environments. Together, this work establishes a framework for probing co-assemblies, revealing that αS-Tau species possess heterogeneous biophysical features and are unlikely to act as a single, uniformly toxic species in PD pathology.

title: Effective stimulation sites and networks for substantia nigra pars reticulata deep brain stimulation for auditory verbal hallucinations in schizophrenia.
abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNpr) is under investigation for managing auditory-verbal hallucinations (AVH) in treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TR-SZ). We assessed acute AVH suppression during initial SNpr-DBS programming in three TR-SZ patients and mapped associated brain network engagement using normative connectomes. One-month post-implantation, monopolar stimulation at each electrode contact was evaluated for its effect on AVH severity. Volumes of tissue activation (VTA) were integrated with normative structural and functional connectivity data to generate individualized network maps. Among 86 VTAs, stimulation volumes associated with greatest AVH relief localized to left anterior-dorsal and right posterior-ventral SNpr. Greater AVH suppression correlated with structural connectivity to sensorimotor cortex and inferior frontal gyral subregions, and functional connectivity to the insula, orbitofrontal cortex, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, regions that fit salience attribution, value/belief updating, and top-down control of source/reality monitoring deficits reported in schizophrenia. These preliminary results highlight specific SNpr subregions and circuits linked to acute symptom reduction, supporting the potential of network-targeted DBS for TR-SZ.

title: Abdominal functional electrical stimulation and binder to reduce orthostatic hypotension in individuals with a subacute spinal cord injury.
abstract: Repeated measures comparative study. Compare acute effects of 4 treatment conditions: (i) abdominal binder (Binder), (ii) abdominal functional electrical stimulation (AFES), (iii) AFES and binder (AFES-Binder), and (iv) no intervention (Control), on signs of orthostatic hypotension (OH) and blood pressure (BP) maintenance in individuals with acute and subacute spinal cord injury (SCI). Spinal injury inpatient ward. Eleven participants with SCI (C3-T5) with at least one sign or symptom of OH underwent a passive sit-up test on 4 days with the 4 treatment conditions. Non-invasive continuous recordings of systolic BP, diastolic BP and calculated mean arterial pressure (MAP) were measured during 4 periods: (1) supine without treatment (5 min); (2) supine with treatment (5 min); (3) upright with treatment (up to 15 min); and (4) supine post-treatment (10 min). Largest drops in BP still resulted in OH in all conditions (p < 0.001), with the largest instantaneous change in MAP in the Binder condition (-41 mmHg [95% CI, -47 to -34]). AFES-Binder condition maintained mean upright MAP relative to supine (-1 mmHg [95% CI, -5 to 2], p = 0.291). Mean upright MAP decreased in all other conditions [Control: (-4 mmHg [95% CI, -7 to -1], p = 0.002); Binder: (-7 mmHg [-10 to -4], p < 0.001); AFES: (-6 mmHg [95% CI, -9 to -2], p < 0.001)]. Mean upright MAP was highest in the AFES-Binder condition. No single treatment condition prevented OH completely. While AFES with abdominal binder does not eliminate OH, it shows potential to mitigate BP instability during postural transitions in acute and subacute SCI.

title: The brain of the female Anopheles gambiae mosquito at spatial and single-cell resolution.
abstract: Blood feeding in Anopheles mosquitoes is at the root of all malaria infections in humans and is supported by a range of physiological and behavioral adaptations. Since behavior is orchestrated at the level of the central nervous system, we surveyed the cellular diversity and spatial organization of the female Anopheles gambiae brain and compared it to other insect species. We then describe transcriptional changes associated with mosquito life history events with single brain and single-cell RNA sequencing. We did not identify expansion of specific cell populations, but a modulation of neurotransmission in the mated mosquitoes, and a metabolic and immune response associated with glia, Kenyon cells and immune cells after bloodmeal, and detected signatures of aging in the mosquito brain. We did not find an effect of Plasmodium falciparum infection. Our atlas will empower the study of non-model insect neurobiology, neural basis of vector behavior, and mechanisms underlying malaria transmission.

title: Functional Capacity as a Correlate of Health-Related Quality of Life in Patients With Heart Failure: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: This study aimed to analyze the associations among functional capacity, self-care, and health-related quality of life in patients with heart failure (HF). A cross-sectional correlational study was conducted. Functional capacity was measured with the Duke Activity Status Index, self-care with the European Heart Failure Self-Care Behaviour Scale, and health-related quality of life with the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire. Data were analyzed using Spearman's correlation and simple linear regression analyses. Ninety-six patients with HF participated. The median functional capacity was 18.90 (IQR: 9.95-32.30), the mean self-care score was 29.60 (SD = 5.68), and the median quality of life was 51.50 (IQR: 40.00-66.00). Functional capacity was strongly and inversely correlated with health-related quality of life (ρ = -0.700, p < 0.001) and accounted for 40.0% of the variance in health-related quality of life scores. In this sample of outpatients with HF, better functional capacity was associated with better health-related quality of life.

title: Compartmentalized coenzyme A and ferroptosis vulnerability in PKAN and CoPAN.
abstract: Ferroptotic vulnerability may arise from the failure of a local antioxidant defense even when whole-cell metabolite abundance appears preserved. Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN) and COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration (CoPAN), two forms of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation caused by defects in coenzyme A (CoA) synthesis, provide a genetically defined setting for examining this possibility. We propose that impairment of the mitochondrial CoA pool can weaken a CoA-dependent redox defense without requiring a measurable whole-cell CoA deficit, while regional iron burden and oxidative demand lower the threshold for ferroptotic death. This model could reconcile apparently preserved bulk CoA with selective neuronal vulnerability. It is testable, remains to be validated directly in patient-derived models, and distinguishes mitochondrial CoA availability from total cellular CoA as the disease-relevant variable.

title: Brain-derived tau in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid after surgery: a prospective cohort substudy.
abstract: Postoperative increases in plasma total tau (t-tau) protein have raised concerns that surgery can cause CNS injury. Brain-derived tau (BD-tau) is a novel biomarker that quantifies CNS-derived tau. We assessed BD-tau concentrations in plasma and CSF after surgery to investigate neuronal injury and mechanisms driving increases in plasma t-tau. This was a substudy of a previous prospective cohort study enrolling adult patients undergoing hip and knee arthroplasty. We measured plasma and CSF BD-tau and t-tau before neuraxial anaesthesia (baseline) and at 4, 8, 24, 32, and 48 h after surgery and assessed cognitive performance at baseline and 3 months. Biomarker concentrations are reported as median (IQR) percentage change from baseline. Plasma BD-tau peaked at 4 h with a 254% increase (137-382%, P<0.001) and remained elevated by 31% (6-75%, P<0.001) at 48 h. CSF BD-tau was unchanged at 4 h but increased by 51% (21-82%, P=0.004) at 48 h. Plasma BD-tau was associated with plasma t-tau (β=1.09, 95% CI 0.95-1.23, P<0.001), whereas plasma BD-tau and CSF BD-tau were inversely associated (β=-0.71, -0.97 to -0.45, P<0.001). Higher postoperative plasma BD-tau was associated with both higher CSF albumin and worse cognitive performance at 3 months. Early postoperative increases in plasma t-tau are consistent with a CNS origin but not concomitant neuronal injury. Instead, the early plasma BD-tau increase and the inverse association between CSF and plasma BD-tau could indicate a redistribution of tau from the CNS to plasma.

title: Corrigendum to "Promotion from Associate Professor to Full Professor Should Not Be Monolithic: A National Bibliometric Study by Radiology Subspecialty" (Acad Radiol 33 [2026] 4207-4217).
Neurovascular Coupling and Subclinical White Matter Alterations in Young Adults with Migraine without Aura: A Multimodal MRI and Machine Learning Study.
abstract: Young adults with migraine without aura (MwoA) may exhibit subtle white matter abnormalities, but their relationships with neurovascular measures, neurotransmitter distributions, and clinical burden remain unclear. We investigated these multimodal imaging associations in MwoA. A total of 130 patients with MwoA and 110 healthy controls (HCs) were enrolled. Multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was used to quantify white matter hyperintensity volume, free water (FW) fraction, peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity (PSMD), and global neurovascular coupling (NVC); the regional measure was the cerebral blood flow (CBF)/fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF) ratio. Regional CBF/fALFF ratio alterations were spatially correlated with canonical neurotransmitter maps. Correlation, chain mediation, and machine-learning analyses were performed. Relative to HCs, patients with MwoA showed increased global FW fraction and PSMD and reduced global NVC. Decreased regional CBF/fALFF ratios involved sensorimotor, striatal, and cingulate regions. The spatial pattern of NVC abnormalities was positively associated with 5-HT1A, D1, DAT, and GABAergic maps, and negatively associated with D2 and noradrenaline transporter maps. FW fraction, PSMD, and regional CBF/fALFF ratio alterations were associated with migraine-related clinical indices. Random forest yielded the numerically highest area under the curve (0.866). Exploratory mediation analysis indicated that FW and PSMD statistically accounted for part of the association between regional CBF/fALFF ratios and clinical severity. Young adults with MwoA exhibited subtle white matter microstructural abnormalities, reduced global NVC, and altered regional CBF/fALFF ratios. These cross-sectional findings suggest a potentially clinically relevant multimodal imaging pattern but require longitudinal and independent validation.

title: Low TRIM21 signal in Sjögren's: biomarker or analytical interference? - Authors' reply.
Bilateral Versus Unilateral Middle Meningeal Artery Embolization for Standalone Treatment of Unilateral Chronic Subdural Hematoma.
abstract: Contralateral dural supply may leave residual membrane perfusion after unilateral middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAE) for unilateral chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH). We compared unilateral and bilateral MMAE selected as initial standalone treatment, focusing on index-admission surgical rescue and other clinically relevant outcomes. This retrospective cohort included patients treated at 16 centers worldwide from 2018 through 2025. The primary endpoint was index-admission surgical rescue. The original 3:1 and confirmatory 1:1 propensity-matched analyses used prespecified baseline covariates. A composite sensitivity outcome of any retreatment was also examined post hoc. Among 600 patients, 546 underwent unilateral and 54 bilateral MMAE. Bilateral cases had lower baseline radiographic severity and more often underwent general anesthesia and selective distal embolization. Index-admission surgical rescue occurred in 9.5% of unilateral and 0% of bilateral cases (p0.99). Other outcomes showed no statistically significant between-group differences, but postdischarge follow-up was incomplete. Overall retreatment did not differ between groups, although bilateral MMAE was associated with fewer index-admission surgical rescues. These observational data identify, but do not validate, angiographically documented contralateral supply as a candidate selection marker for prospective evaluation but do not establish a benefit of bilateral treatment or support routine bilateral MMAE.

title: Transcranial Focused Ultrasound: Established and Emerging Applications in Neurosciences.
abstract: Transcranial MR-guided high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) thermoablation is an established incisionless image-guided treatment for movement disorders; however, neuroradiologist involvement in clinical decision-making and procedural workflows is highly variable and site-specific. Transcranial low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) is a rapidly evolving non-invasive, image-guided technology for neuromodulation and blood-brain barrier disruption. Compared with HIFU, the optimal protocol, therapeutic mechanism, and safety limits remain uncertain for LIFU. Despite these gaps, LIFU has significant potential for neuropsychiatric and neuro-oncologic diseases. Familiarity with transcranial ultrasound principles and the pivotal role of CT and MR imaging for targeting and evaluating outcomes is increasingly important for neuroradiologists. This review uses HIFU as a clinical model to illustrate the integration of imaging into focused ultrasound workflows. We then discuss LIFU with respect to technical factors, imaging considerations, safety, and limitations. We highlight its emerging applications, including neuromodulation, targeted drug delivery, and liquid biopsy. Finally, we conclude by summarizing key knowledge gaps, outlining future directions, and proposing strategies to more actively engage neuroradiologists in this emerging field.

title: Wide dynamic range of contrast-encoding in neural responses in macaque V1.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: The dynamic range of contrast-encoding in the early visual system has been investigated at both single-neuron and population levels in animals using oriented stimuli such as gratings and Gabor patches. However, contrast-encoding of unoriented stimuli such as Gaussians has been less explored, even though such stimuli can evoke a large population response. In studies that employ Gaussians, contrast response functions (CRFs) of neurons and neural populations in primary visual cortex are typically characterized across a limited range of Weber contrasts up to 100%, which may not adequately reflect the statistics of contrast in natural scenes. Indeed, our preliminary analysis shows that locations with center-surround contrasts far exceeding the level comparable to a Gaussian stimulus of 100% Weber contrast are ubiquitous in natural scenes. Thus, our current understanding of contrast encoding remains incomplete in the context of natural environments. Here, we measured spiking activities of individual neurons using electrophysiology and population responses using widefield calcium imaging in V1 of fixating male macaques (Macaca mulatta) while Gaussian stimuli were presented over a wide range of Weber contrasts, up to 900%. Both the average spiking response and the average population response continued to increase robustly above 100% Weber contrast. Only a small minority of neurons saturated below 100% Weber contrast. These results demonstrate that the dynamic range of contrast-encoding in V1 is broader than previously assumed and aligns more closely with the statistics of contrast in natural scenes.Significance Statement The dynamic range of contrast-encoding in V1 has typically been characterized using only a limited range of contrasts, often excluding the high contrasts commonly found in natural scenes. We measured contrast response functions of individual neurons and neural populations in V1 across a much wider range of contrasts. We found that the responses of the majority of neurons, as well as the overall population, increased robustly up to extremely high contrasts. These findings suggest that the dynamic range of contrast encoding in V1 extends well beyond the commonly tested range.

title: Fast corrective responses in redundant motor control are shaped by intrinsic constraints of movement patterns.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: In real-world motor tasks, body movements unfold in a high-dimensional space, whereas task errors are defined in a lower-dimensional space. How such low-dimensional errors propagate across redundant motor degrees of freedom to generate rapid corrective responses remains poorly understood. To address this question, we developed a redundant bimanual task in which human participants (males and females) manipulated a virtual stick with both hands to move its tip to a visual target. By shifting the tip position (task-relevant perturbation) or rotating the stick with the tip position fixed (task-irrelevant perturbation), we separated task-space errors from redundant-dimension errors. Participants rapidly corrected both types of perturbations using highly stereotyped movement patterns. Corrections to task-relevant errors consistently involved coordinated changes across redundant dimensions, and even perturbations that did not affect task success elicited systematic corrective responses. Together, these results demonstrate that fast corrective responses in redundant motor control are shaped by intrinsic coordination constraints that govern how visual errors propagate through the motor system.Significance Statement The motor system can correct a movement error within 200 ms of its occurrence. However, the compensatory movement pattern is not uniquely determined because of the many degrees of freedom in the body. How does the motor system rapidly select and execute an appropriate corrective pattern? Our bimanual stick-tip reaching task, in which participants controlled a cursor located at the tip of a virtual stick, allowed us to dissociate tip-displacing errors from stick-rotation errors. Tip displacements triggered fast corrections, but surprisingly, rotation-only perturbations also evoked rapid responses and biased the tip along its usual coordination between tip motion and stick tilt. Our findings show that fast corrections are constrained by intrinsic coordination patterns, limiting the ability to ignore goal-irrelevant perturbations.

title: Insulin regulates activity-dependent mitochondrial depolarization and calcium dynamics in dentate granule cells.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Systemic insulin resistance is associated with reduced hippocampal energy metabolism and cognitive impairment both in humans and animal models. However, whether insulin rapidly regulates neuronal metabolic stability during activity remains unclear. Here, we examined insulin signaling and queried the corresponding mitochondrial responses in dentate granule cells (DGCs) of adult female mice. This layer of excitatory neurons within the hippocampus plays an essential role in learning and memory. Insulin robustly increased Akt phosphorylation in dentate gyrus tissue when insulin degradation was inhibited, and this response was attenuated by genetic deletion of the insulin receptor in DGCs, consistent with cell-autonomous signaling. We found that insulin did not alter mitochondrial membrane potential at rest, but significantly limited activity-evoked mitochondrial depolarization induced by neuronal stimulation. However, this change had no measurable impact on cytosolic ATP availability and was instead associated with Ca2+ dynamics. Removing Ca2+ ions from the extracellular solution, or disrupting mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake, prevented insulin modulation of the mitochondrial membrane potential. Furthermore, insulin limited cytosolic Ca2+ accumulation through an insulin receptor-dependent mechanism that persisted despite Akt inhibition. Insulin also accelerated the clearance of mitochondrial Ca2+ transients in active neurons, which occurred without changes in either neuronal excitability or pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphorylation. Together, these findings identify endogenous insulin degradation as a key regulator of hippocampal insulin signaling, and reveal a previously unrecognized interaction between insulin and Ca2+ signaling in stimulated DGCs. This work also establishes a direct link between central insulin signaling and the maintenance of mitochondrial electrochemical homeostasis in the adult brain.Significance Statement Insulin signaling is known to influence synaptic plasticity, yet its direct effects on neuronal metabolism remain poorly defined. Here, we show that endogenous insulin degradation limits insulin signaling in adult hippocampal tissue. This finding suggests that inhibitors of the insulin degrading enzyme may hold the potential to improve the efficacy of insulin-based interventions aimed at improving learning and memory. Acute insulin signaling does not modify neuronal excitability, or cytosolic ATP availability. Instead, it stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential and reduces calcium accumulation in active dentate granule cells. By identifying an insulin-dependent mechanism that regulates the electrochemical homeostasis of mitochondria in active neurons, this work provides insight into how brain insulin resistance may contribute to cognitive dysfunction in aging and neurometabolic disorders.

title: Prefrontal ensembles represent freezing of conspecifics.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Social buffering is a process in which the presence of other members of the same species (conspecifics) decreases stress reactions during threat exposure. In parallel, prior reports showed that groups of individuals display synchronous actions in non-threatening situations. However, it is unknown if individuals also synchronize actions when facing threats. Prior studies showed social buffering of freezing in pairs of subjects. We now expand these findings and show social buffering of freezing during exposure to a predator and a shock grid in mice of both sexes in a larger group of four conspecifics. Furthermore, mice also displayed synchronized freezing. The presence of freezing synchrony suggests the existence of a neural representation of conspecific freezing. We reasoned that this encoding might be in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), as this region has been implicated in social behaviors and freezing. Strikingly, mPFC neural activity represented the average level of freezing across conspecifics. MPFC ensembles displayed differential encoding of self and conspecific freezing, and during predator exposure the mPFC encoded the number of conspecifics freezing and conspecific freezing bout duration. These data show, for the first time, neural representation of conspecific freezing, and suggest that the mPFC may coordinate behavioral responses to threat across conspecifics.Significance Statement Social animals display attenuated threat-elicited responses when encountering threats as a group. However, it is unknown how freezing signals from conspecifics are encoded by the brain when facing threats, as prior work has been limited to studies of pairs, or assays without social interactions. We identify a neural population in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) that represents conspecific freezing during grouped threat exposure, and these cells dynamically represent the duration of other animals' freezing bouts. Strikingly, the activity of these ensembles also represents the number of conspecifics freezing. These findings uncover a previously unknown function of the mPFC to encode conspecific freezing.

title: A pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts hippocampal synapse maturation and homeostasis.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are critical for activity-dependent synapse maturation and circuit development. De novo missense mutations in AMPAR subunits are linked to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), yet how these variants disrupt neuronal function remains unclear. Here, we examine a recurrent pathogenic mutation in the GluA1 subunit (GRIA1 p.A636T) that alters AMPAR function and is associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using GluA1A636T knock-in mice of either sex, we identify impairments in hippocampal-dependent learning and working memory. Quantitative proteomics combined with bulk RNA-seq revealed age-dependent molecular remodeling in mutant hippocampus. Synaptic protein alterations were present in juvenile and adult mice, whereas a pronounced upregulation of mitochondrial and glial-associated proteins emerged more strongly in adulthood. Transcriptomic analyses showed partial concordance and highlighted divergence between RNA and protein regulation. Consistent with these molecular changes, there were increases in markers of oxidative stress in juvenile and adult mutant animals, whereas altered mitochondria morphology emerged selectively in adult mutants. Electrophysiological recordings demonstrated reduced basal excitatory transmission, persistence of silent synapses in adulthood and exaggerated activity-dependent synaptic potentiation, which were associated with reduced spine size consistent with impaired synapse maturation. Together, these findings indicate that a pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts developmental synapse maturation with secondary metabolic adaptations emerging over time.Significance Statement Mutations in genes encoding AMPA-type glutamate receptors are increasingly linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism and intellectual disability. However, how these mutations disrupt brain function and development remains poorly understood. Using a mouse model carrying a recurrent disease-associated mutation in the GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit, we show that the presence of this mutant subunit protein impairs the normal maturation of excitatory synapses in the hippocampus. Mutant mice retain immature "silent" synapses into adulthood, exhibit abnormal synaptic plasticity, reduced spine size, and deficits in learning and memory. Molecular analyses reveal age-dependent remodeling of synaptic and mitochondrial proteins, suggesting that metabolic changes arise secondary to disrupted synapse development. These findings clarify how pathogenic AMPA receptor variants alter brain function over time.

title: Specific regulation of transsynaptic nanoalignment and postsynaptic assembly by a novel NCAM family synaptic adhesion molecule.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Synapse formation underlies the organization of neurons into functional circuits and requires precise alignment and coordinated maturation of pre- and postsynaptic compartments. Many synaptogenic adhesion molecules have been identified that drive target recognition and sustained adhesion between appropriate synaptic partners. Yet the degree to which individual molecules serve distinct functions in synapse formation and maturation remains poorly understood. In particular, how exquisite nanoalignment of pre- and postsynaptic specializations flows from micron-scale adhesive interactions between synaptic partners remains a key unanswered question. Here we shed new light on this question by establishing a specialized set of synaptic functions for Epithelial limiter of Fasciclin II function (Elff), an NCAM family member with previously unknown roles in the nervous system. Our structural and functional studies at the glutamatergic Drosophila NMJ of both sexes indicate that Elff is required for postsynaptic function and maturation as well as transsynaptic alignment; however, it is not required for presynaptic function, bouton formation, or developmental expansion of the NMJ. NMJs in elff null mutants display reduced glutamate receptor clusters beginning at the embryonic stage when NMJ synapses first form. Using super-resolution STED microscopy, we demonstrate that these poorly defined postsynaptic specializations are frequently out of register with presynaptic release sites. Surprisingly, the striking defects in elff nulls occur in the context of both normal active zone number and developmental expansion of the NMJ. These findings suggest an unexpected degree of specialization among transsynaptic adhesion complexes and demonstrate that Elff-mediated signaling is critical for transsynaptic nanoarchitecture of glutamatergic synapses.Significance Statement This work reveals a surprisingly selective role for a novel NCAM family member called Elff in coordinating postsynaptic assembly and precise transsynaptic nanoalignment without altering NMJ formation, expansion or presynaptic active zone number. This separation of phenotypes is new and provides crucial insight into molecular specialization of adhesion complexes during synaptogenesis. Because NCAM family member dysfunction linked to multiple neurological disorders, most notably schizophrenia, illuminating the molecular mechanisms by which they orchestrate synaptic organization and function is an important goal.

title: Late Integration of Prior Expectations During Precision-Weighted Perceptual Decisions.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Adaptive perceptual decision-making relies on the ability to combine sensory evidence with prior expectations in a precision-weighted manner. Although Bayesian inference provides a clear normative account of how such integration should occur, the neural mechanisms through which the brain represents and combines priors and likelihoods remain poorly understood. Across two preregistered experiments, we investigated how the precision of learned priors and sensory likelihoods influence visual motion judgements and associated neural activity patterns during a random-dot motion estimation task. Neurotypical adult participants (N=80, 58 female) reported directions of visual motion stimuli, with motion coherence varying randomly across trials. Prior expectations over the continuous motion direction space were manipulated block-wise by implicitly varying the probabilities with which different motion directions were presented. Consistent with precision-weighted inference, response accuracy improved as motion coherence increased with robust response biases toward the expected motion direction. Neural activity measured using electroencephalography (EEG) revealed reliable effects of prior expectation on the univariate central-parietal positivity (CPP), consistent with reduced accumulation of sensory evidence under informative priors. Multivariate analysis using inverted-encoding models revealed robust effects of prior precision on stimulus-specific neural representations, but only late, during response planning stages. Together, these findings suggest that priors learned over a continuous space do not modulate the encoding of sensory evidence and are instead integrated later in the decision-process.Significance Statement Perceptual decisions require combining noisy sensory input with prior expectations about what is likely to occur. It remains unclear how the brain integrates prior expectations with incoming sensory evidence. Using a visual motion task and concurrent brain imaging, we show that expectations do not alter early stimulus-encoding, but are instead integrated at later stages of decision formation and action planning. These findings add nuance to influential theories proposing that learned expectations directly affect stimulus representations and instead highlight their contribution to later decision-related processes. This work advances understanding of how the brain uses experience to optimise perceptual decisions under uncertainty.

title: Representation of emotional expressions across the face and voice brain networks.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Recognizing emotions from faces and voices is fundamental to successful social interaction, yet how the brain represents emotional information across sensory systems remains unclear. Here, we systematically mapped the contribution of individually-defined face- and voice-selective cortical regions in 24 human participants of either sex to unimodal and crossmodal emotion expressions. Using multivariate pattern classification, we show that emotional expressions are robustly decodable from the dominant sensory modality across all individually defined face- and voice-selective areas, and that these representations cannot be accounted for by low- and mid-level stimulus properties alone. Strikingly, emotional information from the non-dominant modality-vocal expressions within face networks and facial expressions within voice networks-was also represented throughout the network, with the exception of the occipital face areas. Crossmodal decoding further revealed a shared neural code for facial and vocal emotions in the temporal voice areas, posterior superior temporal sulcus, and precentral gyrus, indicating that these regions contain emotion representations that generalize across sensory modalities. Furthermore, in most face- and voice-selective regions, audiovisual emotional expressions could be distinguished from representations elicited by the dominant unimodal modality, indicating that bimodal signals are not simply represented as their strongest sensory component. Together, these findings reveal that emotion representations are distributed broadly across face- and voice-selective regions and identify temporo-frontal regions as key sites supporting modality-independent emotion representations.Significance statement Recognizing emotions from faces and voices is essential for everyday social interaction, yet the brain mechanisms that integrate these signals remain poorly understood. Using functional MRI (fMRI) and advanced pattern analyses, we show that emotional expressions are represented widely across both face- and voice-selective brain regions-even when conveyed through a non-preferred sensory modality. Strikingly, specific temporo-frontal regions encode facial and vocal emotions using a partially shared, modality-independent neural code. We further demonstrate that seeing and hearing emotions together reshapes how emotional information is organized in the brain, revealing a graded transition from sensory-specific to multisensory representations. These findings challenge strictly segregated models of emotion processing and provide a more integrated account of how the brain supports social understanding.

title: From data to wisdom: A new era of scientific inquiry.
abstract: Rapid advances in high-throughput technologies and computational tools have ushered in a transformative era for scientific discovery. However, the acceleration of data generation has outpaced our conceptual frameworks for interpreting it. By examining current challenges in drug discovery, phenotypic screening, and model transferability, I argue that the future of scientific integrity depends on our ability to balance technical proficiency with the classical principles of hypothesis negation. Because the scientists who interpret data are themselves prone to bias and error, these safeguards must apply to human judgment as rigorously as to computational tools. I also confront a central tension: the mechanistic understanding I advocate may not scale to systems of cellular complexity. Finally, I propose a collaborative training approach that sustains both experimental excellence and theoretical depth. Each challenge maps onto the Data-Information-Knowledge-Wisdom (DIKW) hierarchy: failures at the D→I transition (underdetermined models), at I→K (undefined null hypotheses and black-box modeling), at K→W (non-transferable animal models and cross-domain blindness), or in the collapse of the entire chain when paradigm inertia forecloses the revision that wisdom demands.

title: Prognostic Value of Sudomotor Small-Fiber Function and Large Nerves for Accelerated Renal Decline in Type 2 Diabetes: A Real-World Cohort Study.
abstract: To evaluate the longitudinal prognostic value of small- and large-fiber peripheral nerve assessments for accelerated renal decline in patients with Type 2 diabetes (T2D). An initial cross-sectional analysis evaluated concurrent neuro-renal associations, while a subsequent longitudinal cohort assessed accelerated renal progression (eGFR loss > 3 mL/min/1.73 m2/year) using paired baseline and follow-up data. Prognostic predictors were selected via LASSO regression. Model utility was assessed using area under the curve (AUC), net reclassification improvement (NRI), and decision curve analysis (DCA). Cross-sectional sudomotor small-fiber dysfunction accurately mirrored concurrent renal impairment (β = 0.18, 95% CI: 0.10-0.26, p < 0.001). Longitudinally, ESCF demonstrated no independent prognostic value for accelerated renal decline, and its apparent longitudinal association with future eGFR was completely attenuated after adjusting for baseline renal function. LASSO regression retained right peroneal motor amplitude, serum albumin, platelet count, and SGLT2i use as robust prognostic factors. Notably, subgroup analyses revealed this large-nerve predictive capacity was significant primarily in patients with established DKD (p for interaction = 0.006). Incorporating this neurofunctional phenotype into standard clinical models yielded a modest AUC improvement but achieved a clinically relevant continuous NRI of 30.35%, successfully recalibrating risk profiles. DCA confirmed a superior net clinical benefit. A distinct prognostic dissociation exists within the diabetic neuro-renal axis. Sudomotor small-fiber dysfunction primarily reflects established microvascular impairment, whereas large motor nerve degeneration demonstrates independent prognostic value for future accelerated renal decline. Incorporating this neurofunctional phenotype into traditional clinical models yields substantial individualized risk reclassification, thereby potentially aiding in identifying high-risk individuals.

title: Cortex-wide imaging in naturally behaving mice with 1-gram wireless mesoscopes.
abstract: Revealing how distributed cortical circuits coordinate behavior in freely moving animals remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience, constrained by limited fields of view, low throughput, and the tethering required by current miniaturized microscopes1-4. Here, we present Airscope, a wireless mesoscope delivering 4 μm lateral resolution across a 6 mm field of view at 12.5 Hz, weighing 1.0 gram. An aspheric-lens design achieves a 2.84× shorter total track length than previous miniaturized microscopes1,2,5,6 while matching the neuron yield of benchtop one-photon mesoscopes; a tailored wireless link supports cable-free calcium imaging from >8,500 neurons per animal (25‑fold increase). Paired with a zero-shot behavior analyzer, Airscope enables cortical imaging across rich behavioral conditions, including room-scale enriched arenas, swimming assays, and multi-organ implantation, with concurrent recording from multiple animals. Using Airscope, we demonstrate versatile applications of untethered cortical imaging across diverse behavioral paradigms. We identify cortical activity patterns across multiple dorsal regions that correlate with behavioral signatures of social dominance, and show dorsal-cortical population activity prospectively decodes competition outcomes across paired animals. We observe reward-location-associated cortical activity patterns during maze exploration, and characterize Granger-causal influence from spinal cord to cortex during fear conditioning, enabled by simultaneous brain-spinal recordings. By uniting large-scale, cellular-resolution recording with unconstrained behavior, Airscope makes naturalistic, multi-animal cortical recording experimentally practical, and provides a broadly accessible technology for systems neuroscience.

title: MRI Characterization of Structural Brain Abnormalities in NGLY1 Deficiency.
journal: International journal of developmental neuroscience : the official journal of the International Society for Developmental Neuroscience
abstract: NGLY1 (N-Glycanase 1) deficiency is an ultrarare autosomal recessive disorder affecting ~165 patients worldwide, characterized by developmental delay, hyperkinetic movement disorders and shortened life expectancy. Despite its severe neurological manifestations, comprehensive neuroimaging characterization has been limited to case reports and small descriptive studies. Our objective was to investigate alterations in brain morphology in patients with NGLY1 deficiency and determine whether these metrics associate with clinical phenotypes. This case series analysed real-world MRI scans performed on 11 patients with molecularly diagnosed NGLY1 deficiency between 1999 and 2023 at sites across the globe. Ages ranged from 2 to 19 years at scan time (five female and six male). Cortical and subcortical morphology, including subcortical volume and cortical thickness, surface area, volume and curvature, was measured with three-dimensional T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. Z scores were calculated using normative models from CentileBrain for patients > 3 years old or custom models for patients < 3 years old. Clinical phenotypes were matched to Human Phenotype Ontology codes. Sixteen scans from 11 patients met quality criteria for analysis. Both age groups (under and over 3 years old) showed significantly reduced subcortical volumes, particularly in bilateral thalamus and putamen. Younger patients demonstrated widespread reductions in cortical surface area, volume and curvature, indicating altered gyrification patterns. Older patients showed thinner dorsal and thicker ventral cortical regions with limited surface area reductions. Thalamic volume reduction in older patients correlated with gait disturbance, dysphagia and EEG abnormalities, with additional cortical associations with sleep and hearing abnormalities. Seizure presence in younger patients correlated with altered cortical thickness, surface area and curvature patterns. NGLY1 deficiency is associated with pervasive alterations in brain development affecting both subcortical and cortical morphology. Age-dependent patterns of cortical alterations indicate disrupted neurodevelopmental trajectories that may reflect impaired neuronal migration and/or altered synaptic pruning. Correlations with clinical variables suggest that these measures may serve as useful biomarkers for tracking disease progression and/or treatment efficacy. These findings provide a comprehensive neuroimaging characterization of NGLY1 Deficiency and establish a foundation for understanding brain structure-function relationships in this ultrarare disorder.

title: Association of early life adversity and peer victimisation with psychopathology and inflammatory-metabolic risk in adolescents from the eBRAIN study: the role of sex and diet.
abstract: Adolescence is a sensitive developmental period during which psychosocial stress can become biologically embedded, increasing risk for psychopathology and inflammatory-metabolic dysregulation. Early life adversity (ELA, such as maltreatment and household dysfunction) and peer victimisation frequently co‑occur, yet their cumulative association with adolescent psychopathology and inflammatory-metabolic risk remains poorly understood. Diet may be a modifiable pathway linking stress to both psychopathology and inflammatory and metabolic processes, yet evidence integrating multiple adversities with both subjective and objective dietary measures is limited. This study aimed to investigate whether co-occurring ELA and peer victimisation were associated with adolescent psychopathology and inflammatory-metabolic markers, and to test whether diet mediated these associations. In an ethically and socio-economic diverse community sample of adolescents (N = 230, age: 12.9 ± 0.9 years), we assessed: 1) exposure to ELA and peer victimisation via structured interviews; 2) Internalising and externalising symptoms, using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ); 3) Age‑adjusted body mass index (BMI) and plasma levels of C‑reactive protein (CRP), as indicators of metabolic and inflammatory risk; and 4) Diet, using self‑reported dietary intake from a Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ) and urinary metabolic signatures of diet from spot urine samples measured via ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography and triple-quadrupole mass spectrometry (UHPLC-Q-q-Q MS). Linear regression models examined the associations between multiple exposures to ELA and peer victimisation with psychopathology, CRP and age-adjusted BMI, and mediation models tested the role of diet. Participants exposed to both ELA and peer victimisation showed more internalising (B = 3.3, 95%CI: 2.0 to 4.6) and externalising symptoms (B = 3.9, 95%CI: 2.5 to 5.3), higher log10CRP (B = 0.4, 95%CI: 0.1 to 0.7) and age-adjusted BMI (B = 1.0, 95%CI: 0.3 to 1.6), and a higher likelihood of unhealthy dietary patterns (76% vs. 51%, pairwise p = 0.020), compared to those with no exposure. However, urinary metabolic signatures were not associated with adversity exposure. An unhealthy diet was associated with higher CRP (1.2 ± 3.8 vs. 0.4 ± 0.6 mg/L; p = 0.013), but not with psychopathology, and did not mediate associations between adversity and outcomes. Exploratory sex‑stratified analyses suggested that associations between multiple adversities and higher CRP and BMI were stronger in boys (log10CRP: B = 0.6, 95% CI: 0.2 to 1.1; age-adjusted BMI: B = 1.2, 95% CI: 0.2 to 2.2) than in girls (log10CRP: B = 0.2, 95% CI: -0.2 to 0.6; age-adjusted BMI: B = 0.6, 95% CI: -0.2 to 1.6), though the moderation effect for BMI did not reach statistical significance, but, again, diet did not mediate these differential associations. Risk for both behavioural difficulties and elevated CRP and BMI was higher among adolescents exposed to multiple forms of adversity, especially boys. Although diet alone may not explain these associations, it remains a relevant target for reducing inflammation and metabolic risk. Future longitudinal research should explore how diet and other modifiable lifestyle behaviours can mitigate the long-term impacts of adolescent adversity.

title: Cross-Modal Masked Connectome Transformer for multimodal EEG-fMRI learning in ADHD diagnosis.
abstract: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is associated with distributed alterations in large-scale brain systems, making reliable diagnosis from neuroimaging data challenging. EEG-derived and fMRI-derived static functional-connectivity profiles summarize patterns of electrophysiological coupling and hemodynamic covariation, respectively, but their heterogeneous signal mechanisms make direct multimodal alignment difficult. We propose a Cross-Modal Masked Connectome Transformer (CM-MCT) for EEG-fMRI based ADHD diagnosis. Instead of imposing direct correspondence between individual connections, CM-MCT treats each Desikan-Killiany 68-region cortical atlas (DK-68) region of interest (ROI) as a connectivity-profile token and learns to recover masked ROI-level connectome information within and across modalities. The model contains modality-specific Transformer encoders, cross-modal masked connectome objectives, and a bidirectional cross-attention fusion module for diagnostic prediction. Cross-fitted mask perturbations are used to characterize ROI-level model dependence, with explicit assessment of associations with nodal strength and perturbation magnitude. Experiments using repeated five-by-five stratified evaluation of 210 paired HBN subjects demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 89.7% accuracy (95% confidence interval: 85.7%-93.3%) and 94.3% AUC (95% confidence interval: 91.5%-96.8%). Compared with the evaluated methods under matched splits, preprocessing, validation, and model-selection rules, CM-MCT shows the highest mean performance, although the AUC difference from the strongest baseline does not reach statistical significance after multiplicity correction. CM-MCT supports multimodal learning from the complementary network-level information provided by static EEG and fMRI connectivity profiles. Perturbation analysis yields modality-specific ROI sensitivity patterns that are modestly associated with the assessed factors. These heatmaps characterize model dependence without establishing causal involvement or identifying ADHD biomarkers.

title: Individualized Prediction of Patient-Defined Treatment Success to Support Patient-Centered Clinical Decision-Making.
journal: Value in health : the journal of the International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research
abstract: Clinical prediction models often target generic thresholds for treatment success, such as the Minimal Important Change. The Personal Meaningful Gain was introduced as a personalized threshold, capturing the improvement an individual seeks to achieve in a self-chosen domain to become satisfied with the treatment results. This study developed and internally validated a treatment-conditional prediction model estimating the probability of achieving the PMG within 3 months in patients with common hand and wrist conditions. This study used real-world data from 25 specialized hand and wrist care clinics in the Netherlands. We included 6263 patients (training data: n=5010; test data: n=1253) treated for common hand and wrist conditions. The prediction target was the PMG achievement at 3 months post-treatment. Model performance was evaluated using discrimination (area under the curve [AUC]) and calibration. The final model was selected based on AUC, calibration, and the number of model features. We selected a gradient boosting machine algorithm with thirteen predictors. The model had an AUC of 0.73 (95% CI: 0.70 to 0.76, indicating acceptable-to-good discrimination) and excellent calibration in the test set. Following a user-centered design, we built a Shiny app visualizing the probability of reaching the PMG for different treatment options (i.e., hand therapy ± injection, injection, or surgery) (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31084375). A treatment-conditional prediction model using a patient-defined threshold for treatment success can provide individualized estimates of the probability of achieving outcomes that matter to patients. This generalizable approach may enhance shared decision-making and expectation management in preference-sensitive care.

title: Heterogeneity in Time-Outcome Associations After Endovascular Thrombectomy: A Binational Registry Study.
journal: Journal of stroke and cerebrovascular diseases : the official journal of National Stroke Association
abstract: Although "time is brain" remains a core principle in acute stroke care, the association between treatment timing and functional outcomes after endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) varies across patients. Some individuals treated in extended time windows still achieve favorable outcomes, a phenomenon termed the "late window paradox." Differences in stroke pathophysiology across etiologies may contribute to heterogeneity in the time-outcome relationship after EVT. We investigated factors associated with heterogeneity in time-dependent EVT responsiveness, with particular attention to stroke etiology. We analyzed data from two multicenter registries in Korea (CRCS-K) and Taiwan (TREAT-AIS) from January 2019 to April 2023. Patients with anterior circulation acute ischemic stroke due to cardioembolism (CE) or large artery atherosclerosis (LAA) were included. Multivariable regression and interaction analyses were performed to evaluate the association between onset-to-puncture (OTP) time and 90-day functional outcomes and to identify effect modifiers. Among 4,719 patients (mean age 72.0 years; 42.9% women; median NIHSS 15), longer OTP time was associated with lower odds of 90-day functional independence (adjusted OR per hour, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.96-0.98; p=0.001). The impact of OTP time varied by stroke characteristics. CE etiology, MCA occlusion, higher NIHSS, and male sex were associated with greater time sensitivity. In CE strokes, each hour of delay reduced the odds of functional independence by 4% (aOR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.94-0.97; p<0.001), whereas no significant association was observed in LAA strokes (P_interaction=0.028). The association between EVT timing and functional outcome varies according to stroke etiology and clinical characteristics, highlighting heterogeneity in time-outcome relationships among EVT-treated patients and providing observational insight into outcome variability in extended treatment windows.

title: Circadian and Sleep-Wake Modulation of EEG Functional Connectivity Across Brain States and Its Associations With Cognition in Humans.
abstract: Sleep and circadian rhythms both influence human brain function, but their distinct contributions to large-scale network organization remain unclear. We quantified the effect of brain state (wake, NREM, REM), sleep-wake history, and circadian phase on functional connectivity using over 1,200 hours of artifact-free EEG recorded during a 10-day forced-desynchrony protocol. We derived principal components of functional connectivity and found that both sleep-wake history and circadian phase significantly modulated functional connectivity, with sleep-wake history exerting a broader influence. Complementary cosinor analyses further demonstrated circadian rhythmicity in several NREM and REM connectivity measures. Across sleep, global connectivity increased progressively during NREM sleep, particularly in the delta and sigma bands, but declined during REM sleep. During controlled resting wakefulness, increasing time awake was associated with higher global alpha-band connectivity, which was associated with poorer concurrent cognitive performance. Connectivity during NREM sleep was also associated with subsequent cognitive performance, with lower global theta and, to a lesser extent, higher sigma connectivity linked to better performance. REM connectivity was not associated with these cognitive measures. Together, these findings reveal opposing NREM and REM trajectories in large-scale EEG functional connectivity and show that these brain-state-specific network dynamics are shaped by both sleep-wake history and circadian phase and are associated with cognitive performance.

title: Amplitude-Conditioned Brain Dynamics Reveal Widespread Negative Modulation and Targeted Positive Modulation of Functional Networks.
abstract: Functional connectivity is traditionally characterized through pairwise interactions between brain regions. However, growing evidence suggests that neural communication is also shaped by higher-order interactions in which the activity of a third region modulates the coupling between others. Here, we introduce a whole-brain framework for mapping resting-state nonlinear conditional connectivity from functional MRI. For each cortical region, we quantified how spontaneous amplitude fluctuations modulate the functional connectivity of all other region pairs. This procedure generated a modulation spectrum for every connection, describing connectivity changes across multiple amplitude states of the modulator. From these spectra, we derived four interpretable features capturing modulatory strength, polarity, volatility, and nonlinear complexity. The framework was applied to resting-state data from the Human Connectome Project and evaluated using stationary surrogate models, spatial topography analyses, test-retest reliability assessments, and behavioral prediction. Surrogate analyses demonstrated that the observed modulation spectra could not be explained by static covariance structure or spectral properties alone, indicating genuine state-dependent dynamic interactions. Topographic mapping reveals a profound functional asymmetry: the macroscopic connectome is dominated by widespread negative modulatory influences, with positive modulation restricted to sparse assortative pathways. Furthermore, by evaluating the effect of temporal integration, we show that spatial and temporal aggregation robustly stabilizes these dynamic fluctuations into reliable, individual-specific traits. Finally, employing regularized predictive modeling, we demonstrate that these dynamic modulatory features can provide complementary predictive value beyond conventional static FC, particularly for capturing state-dependent affective traits such as internalizing behavior. Together, this framework unveils a structured, asymmetric, and behaviorally relevant higher-order modulatory architecture.

title: Multivariate Prediction of White Matter BOLD Activity and Its Relationship to Marginal Connectivity.
abstract: Functional MRI studies have traditionally focused on gray matter, whereas white matter BOLD signals have often been treated as weak or artifactual. However, white matter BOLD fluctuations are robustly detectable and contain reproducible functional information, yet most gray-to-white matter analyses rely on only marginal functional connectivity, which cannot separate pairwise coupling from shared variance among distributed cortical systems. Here, we used a multivariate cortical prediction framework to test whether spontaneous white matter BOLD activity can be predicted from distributed cortical gray matter BOLD activity, and how this predictive structure relates to marginal connectivity. Resting-state fMRI data from 81 Human Connectome Project young adult participants were analyzed using a strict white matter mask with no overlap with cortical predictors. For each white matter voxel, time series from 400 cortical parcels were used to predict white matter BOLD signals with nested leave-one-run-out ridge regression. Cortical BOLD activity modestly but reliably predicted white matter BOLD dynamics, demonstrating consistent cross-validated prediction accuracy across a broad spatial extent of the white matter. Ridge β coefficients strongly recapitulated marginal functional connectivity fingerprints, indicating a shared functional backbone, but their first gradients differed reproducibly. The difference between these gradients defined a β-minus-FC G1 divergence axis that remained stable after broadly controlling for anatomical, signal-related, and spatial factors. At the low end of the axis, enriched in callosal and capsular structures, pairwise gray-to-white matter connectivity was relatively strong, but white matter BOLD fluctuations were predicted less well by distributed cortical BOLD activity than that connectivity would suggest. At the high end, enriched in posterior projection and association pathways, pairwise connectivity was relatively weak, but distributed cortical BOLD activity predicted white matter BOLD signals better than expected. These findings identify a reproducible, tract-organized contrast between marginal connectivity and its covariance-adjusted predictive representation.

title: A shape deformation-based framework for constructing individualized subcortical morphological networks.
abstract: Individualized morphological brain networks have emerged as an important framework for imaging-based connectomics. However, existing methods have focused predominantly on the cerebral cortex, leaving subcortical structures largely unexplored despite their central roles in cognition and neuropsychiatric disorders. Here, we developed a novel framework for constructing individualized subcortical morphological networks from structural magnetic resonance imaging. Specifically, subcortical surfaces were reconstructed using a Point2Mesh-optimized multilayer perceptron architecture and vertex-wise shape deformation was quantified as the signed Euclidean distance between each vertex on an individual mesh and the corresponding vertex on the group-average template mesh. Interregional morphological connectivity in local shape deformation distributions was subsequently estimated using Jensen-Shannon Divergence. Applying this approach to the Human Connectome Project dataset, we found that subcortical morphological networks exhibited complex topological organization, including small-world architecture, modular organization, and highly connected hubs, which were consistently preserved at finer subregional scales. Analyses using an independent test-retest dataset further demonstrated fair-to-good reliability of these network properties. Importantly, these shape deformation-based networks showed significant coupling with subcortical functional networks estimated from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Leveraging large-scale multisite clinical datasets, we further demonstrated alterations of subcortical morphological networks in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder. Schizophrenia was characterized predominantly by right caudate-centered disruptions in morphological connectivity and nodal centrality, whereas major depressive disorder exhibited alterations only in nodal centrality of the right amygdala. Together, these findings establish a novel and reliable framework for investigating subcortical morphological network organization in the human brain across both healthy and psychiatric populations.

title: Aging, Regeneration, and Peripheral Nerve Repair: Integrated Multi-Omics Biomarkers and AI-Enabled Therapeutic Discovery Approaches.
abstract: Peripheral nerve injury (PNI) remains a major cause of long-term sensory and motor dysfunction, imposing a substantial clinical and socioeconomic burden worldwide. Although peripheral nerves possess intrinsic regenerative capacity, functional recovery is often incomplete because of the complex interplay among axonal degeneration, Schwann cell plasticity, neuroimmune responses, extracellular matrix remodeling, metabolic reprogramming, remyelination, and target reinnervation. Recent advances in transcriptomics, proteomics, epigenomics, metabolomics, and single-cell technologies have expanded molecular characterization of nerve degeneration and regeneration, revealing numerous candidate biomarkers and therapeutic targets. However, biological heterogeneity, fragmented datasets, and the lack of robust predictive frameworks still limit translation into clinical practice. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the cellular and molecular mechanisms governing peripheral nerve repair and examine emerging biomarker classes associated with regenerative competence, neuroinflammation, remyelination, and functional recovery. We also discuss therapeutic strategies targeting Schwann cell reprogramming, axonal growth, immune modulation, metabolic adaptation, and remodeling of the regenerative microenvironment. We further examine how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) may support multi-omics integration, biomarker prioritization, outcome prediction, and therapeutic target discovery, while emphasizing that PNI-specific clinical validation remains limited. We propose a systems-level framework that links molecular signatures with clinical outcomes and highlights the potential of AI-enabled multimodal analytics to support translational research. Age-related molecular variation should be incorporated as an additional analytical dimension, allowing comparison of regenerative and non-regenerative signatures across younger and older tissues. Together, these approaches provide a framework for testing age-aware molecular markers and computational models in future translational studies.

title: Validating gene-brain-behavior associations in autism: A replication study.
journal: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
abstract: Autism is characterized by heterogeneity in clinical characteristics, neuroimaging and genetic profiles. To elucidate the multi-level heterogeneity, Buch et al. (2023) identified biologically meaningful subgroups in Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE). However, ABIDE contains non-biological sources of variability due to retrospectively aligned site protocols. To separate biological from site-related variability and test the robustness of these subgroups, we assessed how well their findings replicate in a deeply phenotyped, prospectively collected autism dataset (EU-AIMS LEAP). We included 270 autistic (7.5-30.3 years; 73% male) and 216 non-autistic participants (6.9-31 years; 63.4% male) from LEAP. Regularized canonical correlation analysis (RCCA) was conducted between functional connectivity and three clinical measures (verbal IQ [VIQ], and Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule-2 [ADOS-2] social affect [SA] and restricted/repetitive behavior [RRB]). Next, subgroups identified by hierarchical clustering based on canonical variates were characterized by behavior, functional connectivity patterns and gene enrichment analyses. Three of four autistic subgroups showed behavioral profiles consistent with the original study. Three subgroups shared stronger thalamocortical connectivity, while all four displayed distinct connectivity involving default mode network (DMN), salience (SN), visual and somatomotor networks. These subgroup-specific connectivity patterns were further linked to autism-associated and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-related gene sets. Across preprocessing pipelines, subgroup assignments were partially preserved. Subgroup2 (globally affected behaviors) and Subgroup4 (less social difficulty, but more restricted behavior) retained more consistent behavioral profiles and connectivity alterations, whereas Subgroup1 and Subgroup3 were more sensitive to the precise preprocessing steps. These four subgroups showed partly consistent behavioral profiles, connectivity alterations and genetic patterns, extending our understanding of the multi-level heterogeneity of autism.
